Sample text:
---
# On Mending

There is a drawer in my kitchen that holds the things waiting to be fixed. It contains a lamp cord with its plug snapped off, a zipper pull that came loose from a jacket, three buttons that belong to a coat I wear less than I should, and a small brass hinge from a box whose lid still closes but no longer quite sits true. The drawer is a little monument to intention. Everything in it was going to be repaired "this weekend," and for some of them that weekend was several years ago. I open the drawer occasionally, look at the objects, feel a faint reproach, and close it again.

I think the drawer tells me something about how people relate to damage. We are comfortable with broken things as long as they remain possible to fix. A broken thing that we intend to mend is in a kind of suspended state, neither trash nor treasure, and we can live in that suspension for a long time. The moment we decide a thing will not be repaired, it crosses over. It becomes waste, or it becomes a story, or it becomes something we keep for reasons we cannot quite articulate. Repair is the hinge between those states, and it is worth thinking about more than we do.

---

Mending is one of the oldest human arts, and for most of history it was not an art at all but a necessity. Before cheap manufacturing, a shirt was a substantial investment of labor, and a tear in it was a problem to be solved with thread rather than a reason to buy another. Darning, patching, letting out seams, turning collars, resoling shoes, reattaching handles to pots: these were ordinary household competences, passed from mother to daughter and father to son, practiced so routinely that they barely registered as skills. The worn elbow of a sweater might have been darned so many times that the original wool was almost gone, replaced by a dense lattice of newer thread that was, in its way, a more complicated object than the garment it had been.

We have largely forgotten this. Modern goods are designed, often deliberately, to be difficult to open and impossible to fix. Glue replaces screws. Batteries are sealed inside casings. Software updates arrive on schedules that outlast the hardware they run on. The economic logic is simple: a product that cannot be repaired must be replaced, and replacement is where the profit lives. I do not want to be naive about this. Some of what we call planned obsolescence is real, and the people who lose most from it are the people who can least afford to buy new. A cracked phone screen is an inconvenience for someone with money and a crisis for someone without it.

But there is also a loss here that is harder to measure. When we stop repairing things, we lose not only the skill but a particular relationship to objects. To mend something you have to look at it closely. You have to understand how it was made, where the stress falls, which part is holding the rest together. You have to become, briefly, its student. A thing you have repaired yourself is different from a thing you have simply owned. It carries your hands in it.

---

The Japanese art of kintsugi makes this idea visible in an almost startling way. When a ceramic bowl cracks, the craftsman mends it with lacquer mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum, following the lines of the break rather than hiding them. The result is an object whose damage has become its most striking feature. The cracks are traced in metal, catching the light.

The philosophy behind kintsugi is sometimes described as a celebration of imperfection, and that description is not wrong, but I think it misses something. Kintsugi does not pretend the break never happened. It does not restore the bowl to some original state of wholeness. It accepts that the bowl now has a history, and it makes that history beautiful rather than shameful. The repair is not an attempt to erase the past but an acknowledgment that the past is part of what the object is.

I find this more honest than most of our approaches to damage, whether applied to objects or to people. We tend to want repairs to be invisible. We want the crack to disappear, the scar to fade, the lost year to go unnoticed. Sometimes that is the right goal. But sometimes the most faithful repair is the one that shows its seams.

---

There is an old puzzle in philosophy called the Ship of Theseus. A ship is kept in a harbor for centuries, and over time every plank is replaced as it rots. At the end, not one original piece remains. Is it still the same ship? And if someone collected the discarded planks and reassembled them into a second ship, which one would be the true Theseus?

The puzzle is usually presented as a question about identity, but I always hear it as a question about repair. The ship is maintained, not preserved. Preservation would mean keeping the original intact, freezing it in amber. Maintenance means continuously exchanging parts, so that the ship persists as a pattern rather than as a collection of particular pieces. The ship survives because it is repaired, and in a sense it is constituted by its repairs.

Living things work the same way, of course. Your body replaces most of its cells over the course of years. The atoms you were made of a decade ago have largely dispersed into the world and been replaced by others. What persists is not material but organization, a process of constant mending that keeps the pattern intact. Life is a kind of repair that never finishes.

I find this consoling. It suggests that change and continuity are not opposites, that you can be wholly yourself while being wholly different from what you were. The person who mends a broken thing is doing something close to what the body does, what the ship does, what any lasting thing must do to keep going: accepting that parts will fail and attending to them anyway.

---

Not everything can be repaired, and it is important to say so. Some losses are final. A person who has died cannot be mended back into life. A relationship that has been betrayed beyond recovery may not be repairable by any amount of effort on either side. A forest cut down over centuries does not return in a season. The language of repair can become a kind of moral pressure, a demand that everything be made whole again and that anyone who cannot be made whole is simply failing to try. That demand is cruel when it is aimed at the grieving or the wronged.

There is a difference between mending and pretending. Mending acknowledges the break and works with it. Pretending insists that the break did not happen. The first can be generous; the second is usually a way of avoiding responsibility or pain. A friendship that has been strained can be mended if both people are willing to name what went wrong. A friendship that is simply covered over with politeness will crack again at the same point, and probably harder.

I think about this when I consider my drawer of broken things. Some of those objects I will fix, and I know exactly which ones. The lamp cord is easy. The zipper pull is a matter of ten minutes with pliers. The coat buttons require a needle and a spare hour, which is the real obstacle. The brass hinge might be beyond my ability, and it might be better to admit that and put it in a box for someone who knows more than I do. Honesty about what I can and cannot repair is part of the repair itself.

---

What strikes me most about repair, when I think about it long enough, is how it reverses the usual direction of time. Most of life moves toward entropy. Things wear, fray, rust, and fall apart, and our default is to let them. Repair is a small act of defiance against that drift. It says: this thing is worth another hour of attention. It says: the disorder can be pushed back, at least for now. It is not a permanent victory, because nothing is permanent, but it is a real one.

This is why repair has always been associated with care. To mend something for someone is to say that they matter enough to be worth the trouble. A parent who sews a torn costume the night before a school play, a grandfather who rewires a lamp that belonged to his late wife, a neighbor who fixes a fence without being asked: these acts are small but they carry a message. The message is not "this is perfect now." It is "I am still here, and I am still paying attention."

Maybe that is the deepest thing mending teaches. We are not going to live in a world where nothing breaks. We are going to break things, and be broken by things, and be let down and let others down. The question is what we do afterward. We can discard, or we can attend. We can hide the crack, or we can trace it in gold. We can insist that everything return to what it was, or we can accept what it has become and keep it useful, even beautiful, in its altered form.

---

I am going to take the lamp cord out of the drawer tonight. It is a simple repair: strip a little insulation, separate the wires, attach a new plug, tighten the clamp. I know how to do it, and I have no excuse except inertia. When it is done, the lamp will light the corner of the room where I read, and I will have spent perhaps twenty minutes understanding something I used every day without thinking about. That seems like a fair exchange.

The zipper pull will probably follow, and then one of the buttons. The brass hinge will wait a while longer, and then I will decide whether to try or to pass it on. The drawer will never be empty, I suspect, because things will keep breaking faster than I can mend them. But I have started to think of the drawer differently. It is not a monument to my failures to follow through. It is an inventory of things still in relationship with me, things I have not yet finished caring for.

Every object we own is in some sense a conversation that has not ended. The cracked bowl, the frayed sleeve, the stuck drawer, the sputtering lamp: each is a question about whether we will keep showing up. Answering yes is not always easy, and it is not always possible. But when we do answer, when we pick up the needle or the glue or the thin roll of gold and begin to work, we learn something about patience and attention and the quiet dignity of things that have been used, broken, and kept anyway.

The lamp is waiting. I think I will go and turn it on.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. This is a polished reflective essay, but its recurring kitchen drawer and candid first-person voice make it more personally distinctive than a generic public-intellectual essay.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient, reflective, and gently self-implicating: it begins with a drawer of unfinished repairs and repeatedly returns to it as a way of thinking about damage, care, and time. The essay’s pathos lies in treating attention as a modest but meaningful response to breakage, without pretending that every loss can be repaired. Its invitation is to look closely at what we have set aside, decide honestly what can be mended, and understand care as showing up rather than restoring perfection.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds ordinary damaged objects—the lamp cord, zipper pull, buttons, hinge, bowl—and uses them to connect repair with personal identity, relationships, grief, and environmental loss. It gives moral weight to patience and attention, while resisting the idea that repair must always succeed: some things cannot be restored, and insisting otherwise can become cruel. The choice to end by returning to the lamp makes this reflective argument culminate in a small, concrete act.

## Evidence line
> The drawer will never be empty, I suspect, because things will keep breaking faster than I can mend them.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a distinctive image and a consistent ethic of care, while its polished, familiar reflective-essay structure makes the evidence less individually diagnostic.
